The Dotted gizzard shad Konosirus punctatus is a clupeid species widely distributed along the coastal waters of East Asia, where it forms important components of estuarine and brackish-water fish communities. Field surveys conducted in Japanese coastal lagoons have provided detailed morphometric data for this species, indicating that adults attain a maximum total length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters], a relatively modest size compared to larger clupeids such as the American gizzard shad. Sexual maturity in this species is achieved at a substantially smaller body size, with individuals becoming reproductively active once they reach approximately 15 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15 centimeters] in total length. The transition from juvenile to adult is marked by the onset of gonadal development, and this size at puberty has been consistently documented across multiple populations along the Korean Peninsula and the Seto Inland Sea, suggesting a conserved life-history strategy within the species. This clupeid typically inhabits shallow estuarine zones and forms large aggregations that feed on zooplankton and detritus, playing an important role in nutrient cycling within coastal ecosystems. Its growth rate varies seasonally, with faster increments observed during the warmer months when food availability is elevated.

Reproductive output in Konosirus punctatus has been estimated based on comparative data from the congeneric species Clupanodon thrissa, given the relative scarcity of direct fecundity observations for the dotted gizzard shad itself. When maintained at a water temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C], gravid females are capable of producing approximately 137 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 137 eggs per day], a rate that reflects the maximum reproductive output recorded for this species under optimal thermal conditions. This daily fecundity estimate integrates both the number of oocytes released per spawning event and the frequency of spawning bouts, and it situates Konosirus punctatus among the moderately fecund clupeids, with reproductive investment comparable to that observed in other small-bodied coastal clupeiforms such as Sardinella and Anchoa. The spawning season spans several months during the spring and summer, when water temperatures remain above 18 °C, and multiple spawning events can occur within a single breeding season.

Early life stages of the dotted gizzard shad are characterized by a brief embryonic period that is strongly influenced by ambient temperature. Embryogenesis and subsequent hatching occur after an incubation period of approximately 12.5 days [ab = approximately 12.5 days] when eggs are maintained at 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C], a duration typical for warm-water clupeids with small, pelagic eggs. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva emerges with a very modest body mass; the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0028 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0028 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of the related species Clupanodon thrissa. This minute neonatal mass reflects the substantial energetic constraints faced by lecithotrophic larvae during the critical period between hatching and the onset of exogenous feeding, when yolk reserves must sustain all metabolic demands. The larvae quickly begin feeding on small zooplankton once the yolk sac is absorbed, and their survival during this early period is highly dependent on prey density and water quality.

Adult body mass in Konosirus punctatus exhibits positive allometry relative to length, with the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown individuals reaching approximately 343 grams [Wwi = approximately 343 grams]. This asymptotic mass is derived from length-weight relationships fitted to extensive sampling data, and it represents the maximum recorded body mass for adults within the species' natural range. At the onset of sexual maturity, individuals that have attained the pubertal length of 15 centimeters exhibit a corresponding wet weight at puberty of approximately 34.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 34.3 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required between maturation and the achievement of full adult size. This weight gain trajectory, spanning roughly an order of magnitude from puberty to asymptotic mass, underscores the protracted post-maturation growth phase characteristic of many iteroparous clupeids and indicates that considerable energy is devoted to somatic growth even after reproduction commences.

Longevity estimates for the dotted gizzard shad indicate that individuals can persist for up to 8 years [am = up to 8 years] under the thermal conditions typically encountered throughout their range when reared at a stable temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C]. This maximum lifespan, which is equivalent to approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days], places Konosirus punctatus among the shorter-lived members of the Clupeidae, a pattern consistent with its relatively rapid maturation and moderate asymptotic size at a temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C]. The species' life history is thus characterized by a fast pace of life, with early reproduction, modest maximum size, and a comparatively brief reproductive window, traits that are typical of small, schooling planktivores inhabiting seasonally productive coastal ecosystems where predation pressure and resource variability shape demographic trajectories. These longevity data align well with observations from other small-bodied clupeids that seldom exceed a decade of life.
